transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Octane - Head of ML), Carlos Mendez (Octane - Platform Eng), Sara Li (Octane - CTO)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focused on usage analytics, per-route dashboards and cost breakdown. Customer is evaluating Redwood for a production inference layer for credit-risk models and customer support embeddings. Key concerns: latency SLOs, per-route cost attribution, VPC and SOC2, and ability to run mixed dedicated/hosted routing. Next step is POC with benchmark and pricing.

Topics:
- Per-route dashboards and metrics
- Cost breakdown by model/route/token-level
- Routing policies (hosted vs dedicated)
- Caching/batching and KV cache behaviour
- Security: VPC, KMS, SOC2, audit logs
- POC scope and timelines

Action items (recap in transcript): see metadata

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, Liam our solutions engineer is here as well. Hoy, uh, sorry, go ahead.
[00:18] Priya Singh: Yep, thanks. We're excited to see the console. Quick context: we're running a mix of synchronous scoring for credit models and async embeddings for search, primarily on AWS. We care a lot about per-route cost attribution because compliance asks for a breakdown per product.
[00:32] Maya Chen: Great, that's exactly what today's demo will cover — per-route dashboards, cost breakdown, and how routing works. Liam, wanna take us into the console?
[00:38] Liam Patel: Yeah, jumping in. Sharing my screen now — let me know if the screen share is laggy. Ok, this is the Redwood Console. Top-level nav: usage, routes, models, billing, and ops.
[00:50] Liam Patel: Here on the usage analytics page you can see overall token throughput over time, split by request type: chat/generation, embeddings, rerank. This graph updates almost real time, with a 60s delay for heavy loads.
[01:05] Carlos Mendez: Looks good. Can you break that down by environment? dev/stage/prod?
[01:09] Liam Patel: Yes — we have a filter here for environment, and also by route tag. So you can view only prod routes for a given team.
[01:18] Priya Singh: How do you attribute cost per route? We need that in internal finance reporting.
[01:22] Liam Patel: Good question. So cost attribution is a combination of token accounting and compute attribution. For hosted requests we attribute tokens and apply hosted unit pricing; for dedicated we attribute SRUs based on reserved GPU capacity. You can view cost per route here — it shows token count, compute minutes, and estimated cost.
[01:37] Maya Chen: And important to note — we show both raw cost and amortized cost if you have reserved capacity, so you can see marginal cost vs committed cost.
[01:48] Sara Li: What about caching? We have a lot of repeated prefixes for customer support prompts. Does Redwood show savings from prefix/KV cache?
[01:56] Liam Patel: Yup. Under a route's detail page we have a cache hit rate metric and the derived token savings. Example: 18% cache hit, which reduced token billing by approx 14% last month. We also surface cold-start miss rates and average kv-cache lifecycle.
[02:12] Priya Singh: That's great. Can we see per-model token histograms? For example, we want to know length distributions when routing to a 2k vs 8k model.
[02:20] Liam Patel: Yep — per-route you can drill into token length distribution, p50/p90/p95 generation length, and model variant breakdown. Here, you can toggle model family (gptx-13b / opt-6.7 / redwood-rlm) and see percent of requests to each.
[02:34] Carlos Mendez: A little side Q — our infra team wants to route low-latency traffic to dedicated nodes and fall back to hosted for overflow. Can Redwood do that automatically?
[02:42] Maya Chen: Yes, that's our smart routing. You can define policies by latency SLO, cost threshold, or region. For example, route to dedicated if queue latency < 50ms and failover to hosted if capacity reached. We also support weighted rollouts.
[02:58] Priya Singh: How do you measure latency — end-to-end or just inference?
[03:03] Liam Patel: We measure end-to-end for requests going through Redwood (ingress to token stream completion), and we break down client network, queuing, and inference time in trace details.
[03:14] Priya Singh: Ok. For compliance we need audit logs and per-token data retention policies — can you show that?
[03:21] Liam Patel: Sure — in the ops tab we have Audit Logs (API keys used, request IDs), and Data Retention: you can set per-route retention from 0 days to custom windows; we also integrate with customer KMS for encryption-at-rest.
[03:35] Maya Chen: Pick up on that — for Octane's private deployment we can set up a private control plane in your VPC and either a managed or on-prem data plane. That might be relevant given your regulatory needs.
[03:45] Sara Li: We prefer VPC with our own KMS. Do you support HSM?
[03:49] Liam Patel: We have KMS integrations and HSM via customer key import for enterprise Private. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs in the follow-up.
[04:00] Carlos Mendez: Back to cost — can you show an example cost breakdown for a specific route?
[04:04] Liam Patel: Sure opening route 'credit-score/score-v2' — top shows recent token volume, model mix, average latency, and cost chart. Here you can expand cost components: model token cost, compute amortization (if dedicated), network egress, and caching savings.
[04:18] Priya Singh: Are the token costs model-specific? We sometimes run 2 model families with different per-token prices.
[04:24] Liam Patel: Yes — token unit cost is model-specific. You can set custom model pricing overrides for private or hybrid deployments to reflect internal chargeback.
[04:33] Maya Chen: Also we export per-route cost CSVs for finance — daily or monthly.
[04:37] Priya Singh: Great. For the POC we need to know what observability retention looks like — are traces and per-token logs kept?
[04:44] Liam Patel: Traces are kept according to your retention plan; token-level logs are optional and can be configured to anonymize PII. We support redaction rules.
[04:53] [05:00] Speaker 1: (inaudible) ...
[05:05] Carlos Mendez: One question — do you have a way to group routes by product team? Our finance wants per-product, not just per-route.
[05:12] Liam Patel: Yep you can attach tags (team, product, environment) to routes and then roll up costs by tags. We also have an API to pull tag-aggregated cost data.
[05:23] Priya Singh: For benchmarking, what's the best way to simulate our QPS? We typically run 400 qps at peak with 800 concurrent users hitting scoring endpoints.
[05:33] Liam Patel: We'll set up a POC plan: run an autoscaling test with synthetic traffic matching your distribution. We can simulate both short chat style requests and long generation prompts and measure p95 latency and token throughput.
[05:46] Maya Chen: We'll add that to the benchmark plan. Liam, can you show the per-route SLA breakdown?
[05:50] Liam Patel: Under the route page we have SLA targets and current SLA % over 30d, 7d. For Dedicated customers we provide SLA-backed latency windows; hosted has best-effort but with transparent region-level metrics.
[06:03] Sara Li: Do you offer per-route throttles or quotas? We want to limit experimental teams to lower budgets.
[06:09] Liam Patel: Yes — per-route rate limiting and quotas are first-class. You can set token caps or QPS caps per route, and have alerts when thresholds approach.
[06:20] Priya Singh: A little bit on pricing — how do reserved capacity discounts look? If we commit to dedicated pool of NVIDIA H100s what's the typical discount vs hosted?
[06:30] Maya Chen: Discounts vary by commit size and term; typical reserved capacity reductions are 20-40% on equivalent hosted per-token cost once you amortize the GPU. We'll send exact SKUs and price bands.
[06:43] Carlos Mendez: For the dedicated vs hosted routing — how does fallback preserve request consistency? For example, if dedicated uses a quantized 4-bit model and hosted uses a higher fidelity model, how do you handle output variance?
[06:56] Liam Patel: Good point. We surface model variant compatibility and a policy layer where you can specify compatible fallbacks. You can also set quality thresholds — e.g., only fall back if similarity score > 0.9. We keep versioned model catalogs so you can pin to a set of compatible models.
[07:12] Priya Singh: Can we run A/B experiments in the console?
[07:16] Liam Patel: Yes — rollouts support canary and A/B with traffic splits, and we show per-variant performance and cost so you can measure quality vs cost.
[07:26] Sara Li: Ok, show me the billing export flow.
[07:29] Liam Patel: Billing exports are under the billing tab — daily CSV with per-request token counts, route tags, model used, token price, and cost columns. Also there's an aggregated weekly dashboard for finance.
[07:41] [08:00] Speaker 2: (laughter)
[08:05] Priya Singh: Few more technicals — does Redwood support KV cache warmup or preloading for large context windows? We saw cold-start hits impacting p95.
[08:15] Liam Patel: We support KV pre-warming and explicit cache priming APIs. You can also seed the cache during deploy so the first few requests are warm. For long-running sessions we have policies to keep KV alive for X minutes.
[08:27] Carlos Mendez: What about retries — are energy-consuming retries counted towards cost and how does that show up?
[08:33] Liam Patel: Retries are labeled and you can filter them in the usage export; by default retries are counted as separate token usage but we mark them so you can decide whether to include them in finance calculations.
[08:44] Priya Singh: Any limits on the number of routes? We manage hundreds of micro-routes.
[08:50] Maya Chen: No hard limit — customers run thousands. We recommend grouping via tags for manageability.
[08:57] Sara Li: For the POC what data do you need from us?
[09:00] Maya Chen: Primarily: traffic profile (QPS, avg token lengths, percent embeddings vs generation), a sample dataset for benchmark, desired latency SLOs, and any compliance requirements (SOC2, VPC, KMS).
[09:11] Priya Singh: We'll share that — one more question: do you expose an API to programmatically pull per-route cost?
[09:17] Liam Patel: Yes the Cost API returns per-route/per-tag cost aggregates and raw per-request CSV. We can give you a temp API key for the POC.
[09:26] Carlos Mendez: On observability — can we hook Datadog or Grafana?
[09:30] Liam Patel: We have integrations for Datadog, Prometheus metrics endpoint, and export hooks to S3 for logs.
[09:38] Priya Singh: Ok, shifting back to privacy concerns — what's the default retention on hosted?
[09:43] Liam Patel: Hosted default retention is 30 days for traces and 90 days for aggregated metrics; token logs are disabled by default. For enterprise we can customize.
[09:52] [10:00] Speaker 3: (phone background noise)
[10:05] Maya Chen: Cool, want to show an example of a cost drilldown by tag?
[10:09] Liam Patel: Pulling up tag rollup — here's 'product=payments' — daily cost trend and top contributing routes. You can click into a specific day and see per-request rows with token counts.
[10:22] Priya Singh: If we ship a change that increases token usage, is there an alerting flow?
[10:26] Liam Patel: Yes — you can set budget alerts per tag/route and set actions (email, webhook, slack).
[10:33] Sara Li: For the POC we'd like to try both dedicated and hybrid modes. Is there a setup lead time for dedicated pools?
[10:40] Maya Chen: Typical lead time is 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region; for POC we can do a small dedicated pool or emulate dedicated behavior in hosted with reserved instances for a quicker test.
[10:52] Priya Singh: Ok, timeline question — we want to go to POC in June and decide by end of July if we proceed to dedicated. Is that feasible?
[10:59] Maya Chen: Absolutely — a 4-6 week POC is standard. We'll coordinate with your infra folks for VPC setup.
[11:08] [12:00] Liam Patel: Jumping to the model catalog section — this shows redwood-verified profiles and perf numbers on different hardware. When you pick a model variant we show expected tokens/sec and recommended kernel sets.
[11:28] Carlos Mendez: There's a lot of mention of quantization options — how do we pick them?
[11:32] Liam Patel: The Optimize tab recommends quantization profiles per workload; it takes into account your latency SLO and quality threshold. For scoring where quality is critical we'd recommend FP16 or 8-bit, and for bulk embeddings 4-bit may be OK.
[11:46] Priya Singh: Can we pin a route to always use a certain quant profile?
[11:50] Liam Patel: Yes — route config includes model variant + quantization profile + batching settings.
[11:55] Sara Li: Do you collect eval metrics over time so we can detect regressions after model rollouts?
[11:59] Liam Patel: Yep, quality monitoring is in Optimize — you can attach a set of prompts/evals and get regression alerts if new model variants deviate.
[12:10] Priya Singh: For our compliance team, auditability of rollouts is essential. Is the rollout history stored?
[12:15] Liam Patel: Rollout history, who initiated it, and diff of config are stored in audit logs for 1 year by default, longer retention on request.
[12:24] Maya Chen: Quick pause — any other must-haves we haven't covered?
[12:28] Priya Singh: Just to confirm: per-route cost, ability to pin models, VPC + KMS support, and POC benchmark plan. That's our list.
[12:36] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll send the pricing and SOC2 docs, plus a proposed POC plan. Liam will draft the benchmark and infra checklist.
[12:45] Carlos Mendez: One micro detail — when exporting the CSV, is there a stable request_id we can join to our internal logs?
[12:50] Liam Patel: Yes each row includes request_id, route_id, timestamp, and trace_id so you can join with your logs.
[12:58] Sara Li: Great. Anything else?
[13:00] Priya Singh: No, thanks — that was thorough.
[13:04] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and set up the POC kickoff.

(Conversation continues with minor clarifications and small talk; timestamps below are representative snippets across the remainder of the meeting)

[20:00] Liam Patel: ... and here's an example of the per-token breakdown for an embedding route, you can see prompt tokens vs response tokens and cache savings labelled in green.
[27:30] Priya Singh: Noted. Can you show how to tag a route?
[27:45] Liam Patel: Quick demo — edit route, add tag team:credit, product:loans, save. Tags appear in bill rollups and queries.
[33:15] Carlos Mendez: For security review, we'll need the pen test summary — can you include that in the docs?
[33:22] Maya Chen: Yes we'll include pen test and SOC2 in the follow-up bundle.
[39:40] Priya Singh: One more thing on fallback — do you keep the same session id if fallback happens? We want to track user sessions in analytics.
[39:46] Liam Patel: We pass through a session_id if provided; if the request is retried to fallback model we keep the same session metadata so you can correlate.
[44:10] Maya Chen: Ok wrap-up: we'll send pricing, SOC2, KMS/HSM notes, benchmark plan, and propose POC kickoff dates.
[44:22] Priya Singh: Thanks, looking forward to the benchmark.
[44:25] Sara Li: Thanks all.
[44:30] Maya Chen: Bye everyone.

End of meeting.
